points: The article surveys scientific theories for producing electromagnetic cloaking devices.
A cloak can hide a region of space from passing electromagnetic fields.
A cloak can also hide a region of space from passing sound waves.
A hidden object remains physically present inside the cloaked region.
A basic spatial cloak guides incoming waves around an object so that the object does not disturb the waves.
Some cloaking theories use dipolar scattering cancellation.
Some cloaking theories use sensors.
Some cloaking theories use active sources.
Related cloaking concepts have been proposed in peer-reviewed scientific articles.
Some cloaking theories use electromagnetic metamaterials.
Some cloaking theories use acoustic metamaterials.
Later theories often use metamaterials differently from the original cloak and its successor.
A broadband cloak followed the original demonstration.
The first electromagnetic cloak was produced in 2006.
The first electromagnetic cloak used gradient-index metamaterials.
The first electromagnetic cloak helped spur the development of transformation optics.
Transformation optics controls light propagation by adjusting the properties of the material through which light travels.
Transformation acoustics applies the same principle to sound.
A wave acts on the material through which it propagates.
A simple spatial cloak fine-tunes the propagation medium to direct waves smoothly around an object.
An ideal spatial cloak redirects waves without reflecting them.
The article compares spatial cloaking to water flowing around a rock without producing turbulence.
A symmetrical traffic island illustrates how a flow can divide temporarily and then merge smoothly.
In the traffic-island analogy, the restored flow gives no information about the island's size.
In the traffic-island analogy, the restored flow gives no information about what is on the island.
Both the stream and traffic-island analogies assume a particular direction of flow.
An isotropic cloak works equally well in all orientations.
Cloaks are often designed to be isotropic, but they do not have to be.
The original electromagnetic cloak worked in only two dimensions.
A carpet cloak works from only one side.
In principle, an object can remain invisible indefinitely by staying inside a spatial cloak.
The internal structure of a spatial cloak can trap signals from the hidden object indefinitely if those signals are not absorbed.
If a spatial cloak could be switched at will, switching it off would reveal its contents.
Switching such a cloak back on would hide its contents again.
An event cloak manipulates electromagnetic radiation in both space and time to hide events from distant observers.
The safecracker analogy illustrates an event cloak by having a camera show an undisturbed safe throughout a theft.
The event-cloak concept draws on metamaterials that can make light behave in ways not found in natural materials.
An event cloak uses a medium that can change the speed of different portions of the illuminating light.
The leading portion of the light is sped up so that it passes before the hidden events.
The trailing portion of the light is slowed so that it passes after the hidden events.
The events occur during the resulting interval without illumination.
After the events, the leading portion of light is slowed down.
After the events, the trailing portion of light is sped up.
Closing the gap makes the illumination look continuous to a distant observer.
In the highway analogy, speeding up the cars in front and slowing those behind opens a gap for a pedestrian to cross.
Reversing the speed changes closes the traffic gap after the pedestrian crosses.
The cars represent photons in the highway analogy.
An observer farther down the highway sees uninterrupted traffic and has no sign that the pedestrian crossed.
For an event to be completely hidden, it must not emit radiation.
If a hidden event emits light, a distant observer receives that light as a single flash.
Fluorescence is an example of how an otherwise hidden event might emit light.
One proposed use of event cloaking is to hide interruptions in data channels that meet at a node.
A primary calculation could be paused to process higher-priority information from another channel.
The paused channel could resume without appearing to have been interrupted.
The event cloak was first proposed in 2010.
The first event-cloak proposal came from researchers at Imperial College London in the United Kingdom.
The first event-cloak proposal was published in the Journal of Optics.
The basic event-cloaking concept was demonstrated experimentally with nonlinear optical technology.
The experimental demonstration was presented in a preprint on the Cornell physics arXiv.
The event-cloak experiment used time lenses to slow down and speed up light.
The article describes the use of time lenses as an improvement on the original proposal by McCall and colleagues.
The original proposal relied on the nonlinear refractive index of optical fibers.
The experiment reported a cloaked interval of about 10 picoseconds.
The experimenters suggested that cloaked intervals might be extended to nanoseconds.
The experimenters suggested that cloaked intervals might be extended to microseconds.
A proposed event cloak uses accelerating wave packets to operate in one dispersive medium.
The single-medium proposal avoids the need for two successive media with opposite dispersion.
The single-medium proposal applies a discontinuous nonlinear frequency chirp to part of a monochromatic light wave.
Different frequency components travel at different group velocities in the dispersive medium.
The modulation and dispersion create two oppositely accelerating caustics in space-time.
The shape of the frequency chirp allows the time gap to expand continuously in the same medium.
The shape of the frequency chirp allows the time gap to contract continuously in the same medium.
The time gap in the single-medium proposal is biconvex.
The time gap in the single-medium proposal hides events that occur inside it.
Anomalous localized resonance cloaking was proposed in 2006.
Anomalous localized resonance cloaking matches the resonance of light waves to that of another object.
Around a particle placed near a superlens, the light can resonate at the same frequency as the superlens.
The matched resonance can cancel light reflected by the particle.
Canceling the reflected light makes the particle electromagnetically invisible.
A passive external invisibility device was designed in 2009.
An external cloak can hide an object without enclosing it.
An object hidden by an external cloak can still detect its surroundings.
In an ordinary isolating cloak, electromagnetic radiation cannot enter or leave the hidden region.
Electromagnetic isolation prevents a hidden object from visually detecting its surroundings.
The article identifies the hidden object's inability to sense the outside as a problem that earlier cloaking research had not adequately solved.
An external cloak can hide only part of an object.
Hiding part of a wall could create a virtual peephole through which to see the other side.
In the external-cloak analogy, a broken-down car near a roundabout can force drivers onto different routes.
The broken-down car can also cause a traffic jam.
A deliberately misshapen roundabout represents an external cloak that counteracts the effect of the broken-down car.
In the analogy, the outgoing traffic gives no evidence of either the roundabout or the broken-down car.
A plasmonic cover uses plasmonic resonance to reduce an object's total scattering cross section.
The plasmonic-cover theory applies to spherical objects.
The plasmonic-cover theory applies to cylindrical objects.
A lossless metamaterial cover operating near its plasma resonance could sharply reduce scattering.
A sufficiently large reduction in scattering could make an object appear nearly invisible or transparent to an outside observer.
Plasmonic covers can in principle be passive and operate with little or no energy dissipation.
The plasmonic-cover effect requires materials with low or negative constitutive parameters.
Certain metals near their plasma frequency can supply the required material parameters.
Metamaterials with negative parameters can also meet the material requirement.
Several noble metals have suitable electrical permittivity with relatively low loss at infrared or visible wavelengths.
The article says only microscopic objects could currently be made to appear transparent using plasmonic covers.
The metamaterial in a plasmonic cover can be homogeneous.
The metamaterial in a plasmonic cover can be isotropic.
Plasmonic covers do not need to absorb light to reduce scattering.
The article says plasmonic covers do not require interference cancellation.
Classical metamaterial-cover theory works for only one specific light frequency.
Research by Kort-Kamp and colleagues showed that a metamaterial can be tuned to different light frequencies.
Kort-Kamp and colleagues won the 2013 School on Nonlinear Optics and Nanophotonics prize.
In a tunneling light transmission cloak, light passes through a material with the help of tunneling between resonant inclusions.
A metal film is an example of a material through which light can be transmitted by this mechanism.
A periodic arrangement of dielectric inclusions embedded in metal can produce the tunneling effect.
Transmission peaks reveal mixing and splitting of resonances.
Interactions between the dielectric inclusions contribute to resonance mixing and splitting.
Interference effects contribute to resonance mixing and splitting.
An effective permittivity close to one is the basis of a proposed way to make the resulting material invisible.
A 2007 review identified shortcomings in metamaterial cloaking.
The review presented theoretical solutions that could improve cloaking.
Later in 2007, researchers analyzed in three dimensions a mathematical refinement of cylindrical shielding intended to produce an electromagnetic wormhole.
The electromagnetic wormhole concept is derived from cloaking theory.
An electromagnetic wormhole is an optical device, not a gravitational wormhole.
Electromagnetic wormholes could have applications in existing technologies.
Acoustic metamaterials have achieved negative refraction of sound waves.
An acoustic superlens could improve ultrasound scans.
Acoustic advances could produce more detailed seismic maps.
Acoustic advances could make buildings less vulnerable to earthquakes.
Acoustic advances could reveal finer details in underground images.
Acoustic superlenses, acoustic cloaks, and acoustic metamaterials offer new ways to focus sound waves.
Acoustic superlenses, acoustic cloaks, and acoustic metamaterials offer new ways to steer sound waves.
Acoustic cloaking could hide from sonar an object that would otherwise be detected by the sound it reflects or scatters.
An ideal acoustic cloak would work over a broad range of vibration frequencies.
An ideal acoustic cloak would work across a wide range of physical scales.
Miniature electronic components are an example at the small end of the proposed scale range.
Miniature mechanical components are another example at the small end of the proposed scale range.
Large earthquakes are an example at the large end of the proposed scale range.
Most progress in acoustic cloaking has been mathematical or theoretical.
A metamaterial device that can prevent sonar detection was demonstrated in a laboratory.
The laboratory device can operate with sound frequencies from 40 to 80 kHz.
Cloaking theory has also been applied to waves in water.
A proposed water-wave cloak could protect structures and natural features from destructive ocean waves, including tsunamis.
Artificial platforms are among the structures a water-wave cloak could protect.
Ships are among the structures a water-wave cloak could protect.
Natural coastlines are among the features a water-wave cloak could protect.

question.text: How does cloaking hide objects or events?
options: By moving them out of sight
quotes: hide objects or events by controlling electromagnetic or sound waves
guide or cancel electromagnetic and sound waves so objects or events are concealed
